title: Deploying: containers, orchestration, canary releases
story:
Software that runs on one machine does not run on another, and the reason is that a program's real dependencies are not only its own code. They are every library, binary, environment variable and configuration file the machine happened to have. Works on my machine is a true statement about a set of facts nobody wrote down.

A container packages the process together with those dependencies, so the unit that moves between machines is self-contained. What it isolates is worth being precise about, because the word suggests more than it delivers: it isolates the filesystem view, the process tree, the network namespace and a resource allowance. It does not isolate the kernel — every container on a host shares one, which is why a container is not a security boundary in the way a virtual machine is, and why a kernel-level vulnerability is a host-level vulnerability.

Once the unit is portable, the question becomes who decides where it runs, and the honest history is instructive. Burns, Grant, Oppenheimer, Brewer and Wilkes wrote up the lessons in 2016 under the subtitle lessons learned from three container-management systems over a decade — noting that although widespread interest in containers was relatively recent, their organisation had been managing them at scale for more than ten years and built three different systems in that time, each heavily influenced by its predecessors even though developed for different reasons. The first unified system was built to manage both long-running services and batch jobs, which had previously been handled by two separate systems, and both of those predated the kernel control groups that containers are usually said to be built on. The tooling is younger than the ideas.

An orchestrator takes a declaration of what should be running and works continuously to make reality match it. That is the actual shift and it is larger than it sounds: you have replaced a machine you could inspect with a control loop that decides. During an incident the question changes from what is this box doing to why does the system believe this is correct — and the answer is usually that it is enacting a declaration somebody changed.

Which is what makes canary releases the natural companion. If the system is going to replace instances on your behalf, replace a few first and compare them against the rest while both are serving real traffic. That gives you a control group, which is the same discipline the reliability lesson insisted on — and the comparison must be on a metric users would recognise, because an instance can be healthy by every technical measure while failing the thing people came for.

problem.name: Portable deployment units
problem.shape: Software must run identically on machines whose configuration you did not control and cannot enumerate.
tell: a deployment works in one environment and not another
dependencies are installed by a document of instructions
rollback means redoing a sequence of steps by hand
a new version goes to everyone at once
problem.move: Package the process with its dependencies so the deployable unit is self-contained, declare what should be running rather than performing the steps to make it so, and release to a small fraction first while comparing against the rest on a metric a user would recognise.
problem.invariant: A container isolates the filesystem view, process tree, network namespace and resource allowance. It shares the kernel, so it is an isolation of environment rather than of trust.
problem.breaks: The control loop that keeps reality matching the declaration is itself a system that can be wrong, and it acts continuously and automatically. A bad declaration is enacted faithfully across the fleet faster than a human could have done it, which converts a configuration mistake into an outage at machine speed.

cost.time: image builds and scheduling latency between deciding to run something and it running
cost.space: images stored per version, which is the price of being able to roll back by pointing at an older one
cost.beats: configuring machines by instruction, which is not reproducible, and one machine per service, which is reproducible and wastes most of the hardware

worked.problem: What does a container actually isolate, and what does it not?
worked.reasoning:
It isolates what a process can see and how much it can consume. It does not isolate the kernel, and that distinction decides whether it counts as a security boundary.

What it does isolate, concretely: the filesystem, so the process sees its own root rather than the host's; the process tree, so it cannot see or signal other processes on the machine; the network namespace, so it has its own interfaces and ports; and a resource allowance, so its memory and processor use can be capped. Together those make the environment reproducible, which is the actual problem being solved — the dependency set stops being a property of the machine and becomes a property of the artefact.

What it does not isolate is the kernel. Every container on a host is making system calls into the same one. So a kernel vulnerability reachable from inside a container is reachable from inside every container on that host, and a container escape is a host compromise. That is the difference from a virtual machine, which brings its own kernel and is isolated by hardware. It is why running untrusted code from different tenants in containers on a shared host is a decision requiring a threat model rather than a default.

Two practical consequences follow from getting this right. First, a container is the correct answer to how do I make this run the same everywhere and the wrong answer, by itself, to how do I run code I do not trust. Second, the resource allowance is a limit rather than a guarantee — noisy neighbours still contend for shared caches, memory bandwidth and disk, so isolation of consumption is weaker than the configuration suggests.

The history is worth knowing because it corrects the sense that this is new. The write-up covering three container-management systems is subtitled lessons learned over a decade, and notes that containers had been managed at scale for more than ten years before the widespread interest, with the first unified system built to handle long-running services and batch jobs that two separate systems had handled before. Both of those predated the kernel control groups containers are usually described as being built on. The ideas are older than the tooling, which is why the tooling converged so quickly — it was implementing something already known to work.

problem.practice: Take a service you deploy and list what its container actually shares with its host. Then find the declaration that says how many should be running, change it, and watch how long the system takes to enact it — that duration is how long a mistake takes to reach everywhere.

beats.broke: Software that runs on one machine does not run on another, because what a program depends on is not only its own code but every library, binary and setting the machine happened to have.
beats.fix: Package the process with its dependencies so the unit that moves between machines is self-contained, then hand a scheduler a declaration of what should be running and let it place, restart and replace instances.
beats.cost: You have replaced a machine you understood with a control loop that decides where things run, so the question during an incident changes from what is this box doing to why does the system believe this is correct.

interview.q: What does a container actually isolate, and what does it not?
interview.trap: Treating it as a lightweight virtual machine. It shares the host kernel, so it is an isolation of environment rather than of trust — and the resource allowance is a limit rather than a guarantee, since contention for caches, memory bandwidth and disk persists.
